questions.questionText: Gas exchange in plants occurs through:
questions.explanation: Stomata are tiny pores mainly on the lower surface of leaves that allow gas exchange (CO2 in, O2 out) and water vapour (transpiration) out.

questions.questionText: During photosynthesis, plants:
questions.explanation: During photosynthesis, plants absorb carbon dioxide from air and release oxygen as a by-product of water splitting.

questions.questionText: Transpiration is the:

options.text: Loss of water vapour from plant surfaces

questions.explanation: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plant leaves through stomata, which creates the driving force for water uptake.

questions.questionText: Stomata are most abundant on the:
questions.diagram: Stomata are more abundant on the lower surface of leaves to minimise water loss from direct exposure to sunlight.

questions.questionText: The function of guard cells is to:
questions.explanation: Guard cells control the opening and closing of stomata by changing their turgor pressure in response to light and water conditions.

questions.questionText: At night, plants:

options.text: Perform only respiration, releasing CO2 and absorbing O2

questions.explanation: Without light for photosynthesis, plants respire continuously, taking in O2 and releasing CO2 through stomata.

questions.questionText: The spongy mesophyll layer of a leaf contains:

options.text: Large air spaces for gas circulation

questions.explanation: Spongy mesophyll has loosely packed cells with large air spaces that facilitate the diffusion of CO2 and O2 between stomata and palisade cells.

questions.questionText: When stomata close, the rate of transpiration:
questions.explanation: When stomata close, the main pathway for water vapour loss is blocked, reducing transpiration and conserving water.

questions.questionText: Which environmental factor increases the rate of transpiration?
questions.explanation: Low atmospheric pressure reduces the boiling point of water and increases the diffusion rate of water vapour, accelerating transpiration.

questions.questionText: Light causes stomata to open because:

options.text: Guard cells perform photosynthesis and produce ATP

questions.diagram: Guard cells contain chlorophyll and photosynthesise in light, producing ATP that actively pumps H+ out, causing K+ and water to enter, making guard cells turgid and opening the stoma.

questions.questionText: The cohesion-tension theory explains how:

options.text: Water is pulled up through xylem due to transpiration

questions.explanation: Cohesion (water molecules attract each other) and tension (negative pressure from transpiration) together maintain a continuous water column in xylem.

questions.questionText: Cactus plants have modified stems rather than leaves primarily to:

options.text: Reduce surface area and minimise water loss

questions.explanation: In xerophytes like cacti, leaves are reduced to spines, and green stems perform photosynthesis, greatly reducing surface area and water loss.

questions.questionText: The net effect of transpiration is that it:

options.text: Creates negative pressure that pulls water up from roots

questions.diagram: Transpiration creates a pulling force (negative pressure) in the xylem that draws water upward from roots to replace lost water.

questions.questionText: Which gas diffuses into the leaf through stomata during the day?
questions.diagram: Carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf through stomata during the day for use in photosynthesis (light-independent reactions).

questions.questionText: During drought conditions, abscisic acid causes:

options.text: Stomata to close to conserve water

questions.explanation: Abscisic acid (ABA) is a stress hormone that triggers stomatal closure during drought by stimulating K+ efflux from guard cells, reducing turgor.

questions.questionText: The lenticels on plant stems allow:

options.text: Gas exchange between internal tissues and the atmosphere

questions.explanation: Lenticels are loose, aerenchyma tissue openings on woody stems and roots that allow oxygen to diffuse in and CO2 to diffuse out for cell respiration.

questions.questionText: A plant that has stomata open only at night and closed during the day is described as:
questions.explanation: CAM plants (e.g., succulents) open stomata at night to minimise water loss, storing CO2 as malate, then using it for photosynthesis during the day with closed stomata.

questions.questionText: The rate of diffusion of gases through stomata is directly proportional to:

options.text: The square of the pore diameter

questions.explanation: According to Graham's law, the rate of diffusion through a pore is proportional to the square of its diameter, so small changes in aperture size significantly affect diffusion rates.

questions.questionText: Root pressure is important for:

options.text: Pushing water up the xylem, especially at night

questions.diagram: Root pressure develops from active transport of minerals into xylem, drawing water osmotically and pushing sap upward, particularly important at night when transpiration is low.

questions.questionText: The role of the cuticle in gas exchange is to:

options.text: Allow gases to pass through freely
Form a waterproof barrier, directing gas exchange through stomata

questions.hint: The waxy cuticle covers the epidermis and is impermeable to gases, forcing all gas exchange to occur through stomata for regulated control.
